questions.question: Why can overall accuracy be misleading as a performance measure for a classifier in the intrusion‑detection scenario described in the context?

options.A: Because a classifier that always predicts “normal” will still achieve high accuracy due to the large number of normal samples.
options.B: Because the classifier’s speed is more important than its correctness.
options.C: Because normalization of the data automatically corrects any misclassification.
options.D: Because the intrusion‑detection system uses bitmap indexing, which inflates accuracy.

questions.explanation:
The context explains that normal samples far outnumber outlier samples, so a classifier that simply predicts “normal” can obtain a high accuracy despite being useless for detecting intrusions [Page 127].

---

questions.question: Which example from the context best illustrates the Base Rate Fallacy?

options.A: An intrusion‑detection system where most accesses are normal, causing a naïve classifier to appear accurate.
options.B: A bitmap index that speeds up low‑cardinality queries.
options.C: Normalizing attribute values to the range 0.0–1.0 before mining.
options.D: Scanning a working relation only once to collect statistics.

questions.explanation:
The Base Rate Fallacy occurs when the low base rate of outliers makes accuracy misleading; the intrusion‑detection example in the text matches this description [Page 127].

---

questions.question: Which three elements are identified in the context as defining data quality?
questions.explanation:
The passage lists accuracy, completeness, and consistency as the three data‑quality elements [Page 2].

---

questions.question: How does attribute‑oriented induction potentially limit the usefulness of accuracy as a performance metric?

options.A: It requires scanning the relation multiple times, increasing error.
options.B: Automatic generalization may hide detailed patterns, reducing the classifier’s ability to capture subtle differences.
options.C: It forces the use of chi‑square tests for nominal data.
options.D: It guarantees perfect accuracy by removing noisy attributes.

questions.explanation:
The context notes that attribute‑oriented induction “automatically generalizes data to a higher level” and cannot efficiently support deeper drill‑down, which can obscure details needed for accurate classification [Page 96].

---

questions.question: According to the context, what is a direct consequence of the imbalance between normal and outlier samples when building a classifier?

options.A: Insufficient outlier samples make it difficult to construct an accurate model.
options.B: The classifier will automatically achieve 100 % precision.
options.C: Normalization of attribute values eliminates the imbalance.
options.D: Bitmap indexing resolves the imbalance issue.

questions.explanation:
The passage states that the scarcity of outlier samples “can prevent us from building an accurate classifier” [Page 127].

---

questions.question: In the intrusion‑detection example, why might a classifier with 95 % overall accuracy still be considered ineffective?

options.A: Because the high accuracy may be due to correctly labeling the abundant normal events while missing most intrusions.
options.B: Because 95 % accuracy exceeds the theoretical maximum for any classifier.
options.C: Because accuracy does not account for the speed of detection.
options.D: Because the classifier uses chi‑square testing, which is unsuitable for nominal data.

questions.explanation:
With a dominant normal class, a classifier can achieve high accuracy simply by labeling everything as normal, yet fail to detect intrusions—a classic illustration of the base‑rate problem [Page 127].

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the context as a source of inaccurate data?

options.A: Incorrect attribute values entered during data collection.
options.D: Scaling data to the range 0.0–1.0 through normalization.

questions.explanation:
The text lists reasons for inaccurate data such as incorrect values, incompleteness, and inconsistency, but describes normalization as a technique that can improve accuracy, not cause inaccuracy [Page 2].

---

questions.question: How does a low base rate of outlier events affect the interpretation of classifier accuracy, as discussed in the context?

options.A: It allows a trivial “always‑normal” classifier to achieve high accuracy, masking poor detection performance.
options.B: It forces the classifier to lower its overall accuracy.
options.C: It makes accuracy an ideal sole metric for performance evaluation.
options.D: It eliminates the need for any performance metric beyond accuracy.

questions.explanation:
The passage explains that because normal events dominate, a classifier that never predicts an outlier can still show high accuracy, illustrating the base‑rate fallacy [Page 127].

questions.question: Which processing step described in the context could be directly affected by inaccurate or incomplete data, potentially leading to misleading accuracy results?

options.A: Step 1 – collecting the task‑relevant data into the working relation.
options.B: Step 2 – scanning the working relation to collect statistics on attribute values.
options.C: Step 3 – generalizing attribute values based on desired levels.
options.D: The final indexing of bitmap structures.

questions.explanation:
Step 2 relies on statistics gathered from the data; if the data contain inaccurate or missing values, the derived statistics—and consequently any accuracy assessment—will be unreliable [Page 90].

questions.question: Why might accuracy alone be insufficient when assessing the quality of a correlation discovered by a χ² test for nominal attributes, according to the context?

options.A: Because χ² measures statistical significance, not the proportion of correctly predicted instances.
options.B: Because accuracy automatically improves after χ² testing.
options.C: Because correlation analysis eliminates the need for any performance metric.
options.D: Because χ² tests are only applicable to continuous attributes.

questions.explanation: The context notes that correlation analysis for nominal data uses the χ² test, which evaluates how strongly one attribute implies another; this statistical significance is distinct from accuracy, which measures correct predictions [Page 12].
